newsitem.title: INDIA: U.K. insurers keen to return, aid Indian economy.
newsitem.headline: U.K. insurers keen to return, aid Indian economy.

text.p: British insurance firms on Wednesday said their return to India would result in more jobs, lower premia, deeper debt and equity markets and more funds to boost India's creaking infrastructure.

"The entry of foreign insurers will increase employment opportunities and stimulate enhanced growth in the market," British high commissioner David Gore Booth told a seminar organised by the Association of British Insurers.
Before India nationalised the life insurance industry in 1956 and the general insurance industry in 1972, British firms were well represented in India.
Opposition from political groups including the Communist Party, within the ruling United Front government are blocking efforts to open up the sector.
Gore Booth asked British insurers not be disheartened by the slow pace of opening of the Indian insurance sector. "It is dangerous to forecast timing in India," he said.
"It will probably be sooner rather than later."
The Indian business was the largest overseas operations of some of the British firms like Prudential Corp.

"Fears of foreign domination of the domestic market are unfounded," Gore Booth said. He said the foreign share of life insurance sector in South Korea was three percent and in Taiwan 1.5 percent. Foreign share of general insurance was even lower.
The presence of increased insurance capacity within the Indian market will mean that more premiums can be retained within the Indian industry, he said.
Delegates said new insurers would expand the Indian industry and open up new segments.
Duncan West, chief executive officer of Royal SunAlliance said he was often told thefts were not a major issue in India.
"Even the Punjab National Bank had a raid in Delhi recently and all its safety deposit boxes were looted," West said.
"No insurance cover was in place for most of the contents."
Motor fleet insurance was another area where British insurers could offer their expertise, West told the seminar.
West said U.K. firms had begun work on paperless office in processing insurance claims.
He said even if the insurer's own local office was affected by a storm, say in the storm-prone Andhra Pradesh state, other offices could offer quality service despite the high volume of claims.
Mark Tucker, managing director of Prudential Corporation Asia said life insurers elsewhere stimulate the economy by providing finance to both the government and the industry.
"One of the major problems faced by rapidly developing countries like India is how to raise funds for infrastructure development at a reasonable cost," Tucker said.
Will Hay, head of bonds at Standard Life Assurance Company, said an effective life assurance industry needed an established primary and a liquid secondary market.
India's bond market is Asia's third largest but the secondary market is highly illiquid.

Wendy Hay, investment manager at Standard Life Assurance Company said India's fiscal deficit of approximately 6.0 percent of GDP "is moving in the right direction but is still draining funds from the system."

"Insurance companies are not 'hot money' players. Hence encouraging long-term equity investments by institutions such as insurers seems to me to be a sound bet to secure India's long-term growth strategy," Hay told the seminar.
